NEW YORK (CNN)  -- Obesity is the No. 1 health crisis in the United States, and the nation could be at risk without immediate action, former President Clinton said at CNN's first Fit Nation Summit. CNN's Dr. Sanjay Gupta and former President Clinton lead the discussion at the first Fit Nation Summit. "We need to do something about it for our children, and for our country, because something like this could easily collapse our nation if we don't act now," Clinton said. Clinton and CNN's chief medical correspondent, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, gathered with experts from across the country Wednesday to explore solutions to America's obesity crisis. Two-thirds of adult Americans are overweight or obese; the same is true for one-third of U.S. children, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Obesity carries increased risk of myriad health problems, including hypertension, diabetes, heart disease and arthritis. Gupta, Clinton and a panel of experts addressed such proposed solutions as healthy school lunches, elimination of trans fats, the need for healthier food in urban communities and the importance of supporting community-based efforts to fight obesity.  Watch Gupta explain the solutions proposed at the Fit Nation Summit » . Clinton, who's been tackling the obesity issue over the past few years with his Alliance for a Healthier Generation, stressed the need to help educate people about the importance of a healthy diet and exercising together. Motivating Americans, especially kids, won't be easy, Clinton said. "They need to be handled with care. Kids need to know it's important, but [fitness] can't be boring," he said. "There's no shame, there's no embarrassment. We have to let them know it's all good, but you have to do it." Michael Jacobson, director of the Center for Science in the Public Interest and a strong advocate against trans fats in foods, stressed that the Food and Drug Administration should ban trans fats altogether and stop leaving it up to local and state governments. Trans fats, at one time, thought to be good fat substitutes, over the years have been shown to raise LDL or bad cholesterol in people and lower their HDL, or good cholesterol. "They're just not good for our health, Jacobson said. However, Dr. Robert Eckel, former president of the American Heart Association, warned, "Although we support the removal of trans fats, our biggest concern is what they'll be replaced with. We need to think about that, because there will be a substitute." The panel took questions from an audience of 150 people -- mostly obesity experts or those who work in industries that deal with obesity. Gupta was inspired to launch Fit Nation, an ongoing, multiplatform, grass-roots initiative against obesity. Over the past three years, Gupta and the CNN Medical Unit have crisscrossed the country, asking Americans to take charge of their weight by exercising more and eating healthier. This year, Gupta traveled from Michigan to California asking the public to pledge to add 1 million hours to their collective lives by getting off the couch and exercising. Since he began the tour in April, the campaign has surpassed its goal, with exercise pledges close to four times that amount. Gupta said he hopes that legislators and administrators who can make a difference in policy and perhaps change attitudes about obesity will hear the solutions discussed at the summit. "I''ve covered a lot of stories on obesity," Gupta said. "There's a battle going on, and we need to win the battle. I've talked to people out there and many are just blasé. "This is our opportunity to make them care." E-mail to a friend .

NEW YORK (CNN) -- Speaking at CNN's inaugural Fit Nation Summit, former President Clinton declared that obesity ranks as America's most pressing health emergency, warning that the country faces serious danger unless it responds right away.

"For the sake of our kids and our nation, we have to take action, because a problem like this could bring down our country if we fail to move now," Clinton stated.

On Wednesday, Clinton joined CNN's chief medical correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta and specialists from around the nation to search for ways to address America's obesity epidemic. Figures from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show that two out of three American adults are either overweight or obese, and one out of three American children falls into the same category. Being obese elevates the danger of numerous medical conditions, such as high blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease and arthritis.

During the summit, Gupta, Clinton and a group of experts discussed potential remedies including nutritious school meals, banning trans fats, bringing healthier food options to city neighborhoods, and the value of backing local anti-obesity programs.

Clinton, who has spent recent years working on the obesity problem through his Alliance for a Healthier Generation, emphasized how crucial it is to teach people why healthy eating and exercising together matter. He acknowledged that inspiring Americans—particularly children—would be challenging.

"We have to approach them carefully. Children have to understand this matters, but exercise can't feel dull," he explained. "There shouldn't be any shame or embarrassment. We need to show them it's positive, but they've got to actually do it."

Michael Jacobson, who heads the Center for Science in the Public Interest and campaigns forcefully against trans fats, argued that the Food and Drug Administration ought to prohibit trans fats across the board rather than passing the responsibility to state and local authorities. Once considered a healthy alternative to other fats, trans fats have proven over time to boost people's LDL, or harmful cholesterol, while reducing their HDL, or beneficial cholesterol. "They simply aren't healthy for us," Jacobson said.

Yet Dr. Robert Eckel, who previously led the American Heart Association, cautioned: "While we back eliminating trans fats, our main worry is what will take their place. We have to consider that, since something will replace them."

The panel fielded questions from roughly 150 attendees, most of whom were either obesity specialists or professionals working in fields connected to obesity.

The event grew out of Gupta's decision to create Fit Nation, a continuous, multiplatform grassroots campaign targeting obesity. For the last three years, Gupta and CNN's Medical Unit have traveled throughout the country, urging Americans to control their weight through more physical activity and better eating habits. This year, Gupta journeyed from Michigan all the way to California, encouraging people to commit to collectively adding one million hours to their lifespans by getting active. Since the tour kicked off in April, the effort has blown past its target, gathering exercise commitments amounting to nearly four times the original goal.

Gupta expressed hope that lawmakers and officials capable of shaping policy—and possibly shifting how people view obesity—would take note of the solutions raised at the summit.

"I've reported on plenty of obesity stories," Gupta remarked. "There's a fight underway, and we have to come out on top. I've spoken with people, and a lot of them just don't seem to care. This is our chance to change that."

E-mail to a friend.

# Confronting America's Obesity Crisis

Former President Clinton has declared obesity the number one health crisis in the United States, issuing a stark warning that the nation could face collapse without immediate and decisive action. His remarks underscored the urgency of addressing a problem that has quietly grown into one of the most pressing public health challenges of our time.

The scale of the crisis is difficult to overstate. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, two-thirds of adult Americans and one-third of U.S. children are now overweight or obese. These figures reveal a troubling trend that spans generations, affecting not only today's adults but also the children who represent the nation's future.

The consequences of this epidemic extend far beyond appearance or lifestyle. Obesity significantly increases the risk of a range of serious health problems, including hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, and arthritis. These conditions place enormous strain on individuals, families, and the healthcare system as a whole, driving up costs and diminishing quality of life for millions of Americans.

In response to these challenges, the Fit Nation Summit brought together leaders and experts to explore practical solutions. Discussions focused on providing healthier school lunches, eliminating trans fats from the food supply, and offering support for community-based efforts designed to combat obesity at the local level. These strategies reflect a comprehensive approach, targeting both the food environment and the grassroots initiatives that can drive meaningful change.

Throughout the summit, Clinton emphasized the importance of educating and motivating people—especially children—to embrace healthy diets and regular exercise. Crucially, he stressed that this transformation must occur without shame or embarrassment. By fostering an environment of encouragement rather than judgment, he argued, the nation can empower its citizens to make lasting changes and reverse the tide of obesity before it is too late.

# America's Fight Against Obesity: Highlights from CNN's First Fit Nation Summit

America is facing a health crisis of staggering proportions, and at CNN's first Fit Nation Summit, some of the nation's most influential voices came together to confront it head-on. Former President Bill Clinton joined CNN's chief medical correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta and a distinguished panel of health experts to tackle one of the country's most pressing challenges: the obesity epidemic.

## A Nation at Risk

The statistics presented at the summit painted a sobering picture. Two-thirds of American adults and one-third of American children are now overweight or obese. Beyond the numbers, the panelists stressed the human cost of this crisis. Excess weight dramatically increases the risk of serious health problems, including type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, and certain cancers. For children especially, these conditions—once considered adult diseases—are appearing at alarming rates, threatening to make this the first generation to live shorter lives than their parents.

## Exploring Practical Solutions

Rather than simply diagnosing the problem, the summit focused on actionable solutions. The panel explored a range of strategies aimed at reversing current trends:

- **Healthier school lunches:** With children consuming a significant portion of their daily calories at school, improving the nutritional quality of cafeteria meals emerged as a critical priority. Reducing sugary drinks and processed foods while introducing fresh fruits and vegetables could reshape eating habits early in life.

- **Banning trans fats:** The panelists advocated for eliminating harmful trans fats from the food supply, pointing to their direct link to heart disease and other cardiovascular problems.

- **Supporting community-based fitness efforts:** Local initiatives that encourage physical activity—from safe parks and walking trails to school and neighborhood programs—were highlighted as essential tools for building a culture of movement and wellness.

## The Call for Immediate Action

Throughout the discussion, a common theme resonated: the time to act is now. President Clinton, whose foundation has championed childhood health initiatives, emphasized that meaningful change requires cooperation among government, schools, businesses, and families alike. Dr. Gupta and the other experts reinforced that education is a powerful weapon in this fight. Teaching Americans—both young and old—about the fundamentals of healthy diet and regular exercise can empower individuals to make better choices.

The panelists agreed that obesity is not merely a personal failing but a societal challenge that demands collective responsibility. Left unaddressed, its consequences will ripple through the nation's healthcare system, economy, and overall quality of life for generations to come.

## Protecting the Nation's Future

Ultimately, the Fit Nation Summit served as both a warning and a rallying cry. The experts made clear that protecting America's future depends on the decisions made today. By investing in healthier environments, promoting education, and supporting practical, community-driven solutions, the nation can begin to turn the tide against obesity—and give both current and future generations a healthier path forward.

## Understanding the "NEW YORK (CNN)" Format

When you see **NEW YORK (CNN)** at the beginning of an article, this is called a **dateline**. It's a standard journalistic convention that tells readers two important pieces of information:

- **NEW YORK** – The city where the story was reported or originated

Datelines have been a staple of journalism for well over a century. They serve several purposes:

1. **Establishing location** – Readers immediately know where events took place
2. **Credibility** – Showing that a reporter was on the ground at the source
3. **Context** – Helping readers understand the geographic relevance of a story

### Common CNN Datelines

CNN, being a major international news network headquartered partly in New York and Atlanta, uses various datelines depending on where stories break:

- **NEW YORK (CNN)** – Financial news, UN coverage, major events

# Clinton, Gupta Lead Discussion on Obesity at CNN's First Fit Nation Summit

Former President Bill Clinton and CNN Chief Medical Correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta headlined a wide-ranging discussion on America's obesity epidemic at CNN's inaugural Fit Nation Summit, calling for renewed national efforts to combat what both described as a growing public health crisis.

The event brought together health experts, policymakers, and advocates to address rising obesity rates and their impact on Americans, particularly children.

## A Personal Mission

Clinton, who has become an outspoken advocate for healthier living following his own heart health scares, spoke candidly about his personal transformation and the lessons he's learned about diet and nutrition.

"We didn't get into this situation overnight, and we won't get out of it overnight either," Clinton told the audience. "But I've seen firsthand that changing our habits is possible, and it can add years to your life."

The former president highlighted the work of his foundation, which has partnered with beverage companies and schools to reduce the availability of high-calorie drinks in educational settings—an initiative he cited as evidence that meaningful change can happen through collaboration rather than confrontation.

## Focus on Childhood Obesity

Dr. Gupta, who moderated much of the discussion, emphasized the alarming trends in childhood obesity and the long-term health consequences facing younger generations.

"When we talk about obesity, we're really talking about a range of related conditions—diabetes, heart disease, certain cancers," Gupta noted. "The choices we make about food and physical activity today will shape the health of our nation for decades."

Gupta pointed to research showing that today's children could be among the first generations to have shorter life expectancies than their parents, a statistic he called a "wake-up call" for families and communities.

## Solutions and the Path Forward

The conversation moved beyond identifying problems to exploring practical solutions. Panelists discussed the importance of:

- **Improving school nutrition** programs and reducing access to sugary drinks and processed foods
- **Increasing physical activity** through better community design and school programs
- **Making healthy food affordable** and accessible in underserved communities
- **Empowering families** with education about nutrition and cooking

Clinton stressed that solutions must account for economic realities, noting that healthy options are often more expensive and less available in low-income areas.

"We have to make the healthy choice the easy choice," he said. "That means working with businesses, schools, and communities to change the environment people live in."

## A Broader Movement

The Fit Nation Summit represents an expansion of CNN's ongoing Fit Nation initiative, which encourages viewers to adopt healthier lifestyles. Gupta has been a driving force behind the program, personally participating in triathlons and other physical challenges to inspire audiences.

Both Clinton and Gupta expressed optimism that, with sustained attention and collective action, the trajectory of the obesity epidemic could be reversed.

"This is about giving people the tools and opportunities to live healthier lives," Gupta concluded. "It's a challenge, but it's one we can meet together."

The summit concluded with a call to action for attendees and viewers to become advocates for healthier communities in their own neighborhoods.

---

*For more information on healthy living tips and the Fit Nation initiative, visit CNN.com/Health.*

*Health leaders, former president gather to address escalating epidemic*

WASHINGTON — Health experts, policymakers, and public figures convened this week at a national health summit where obesity took center stage as what many described as the most pressing public health crisis facing the United States.

With obesity rates affecting roughly 40 percent of American adults according to federal health data, speakers emphasized that the condition drives a cascade of related illnesses, from type 2 diabetes and heart disease to certain cancers, while straining the healthcare system and economy.

## A Call to Action

Former President Bill Clinton, whose foundation has long championed childhood health initiatives, delivered remarks framing obesity as both a personal and national concern.

"We have to make the healthy choice the easy choice for American families," Clinton told attendees. "This isn't about blaming individuals—it's about building an environment where good nutrition and physical activity are accessible to everyone, regardless of their zip code or income."

Clinton, who dramatically changed his own diet following heart health scares, has frequently spoken about the intersection of food policy, poverty, and wellness.

## A Medical Perspective

Dr. Sanjay Gupta, the neurosurgeon and prominent medical correspondent, underscored the biological complexity of the epidemic.

"For too long we've treated obesity as simply a matter of willpower," Gupta said. "The science tells us it's far more complicated—involving genetics, environment, sleep, stress, and the food landscape we've created. We need to approach this with the same seriousness we bring to any chronic disease."

Gupta also pointed to emerging pharmaceutical treatments, cautioning that medication alone won't solve a systemic problem. "These new drugs are remarkable tools, but they're not a substitute for the broader cultural and structural changes we need."

Other experts echoed the urgency while highlighting specific solutions.

"The economic cost is staggering—we're talking about hundreds of billions annually in medical expenses and lost productivity," said one public health researcher presenting at the summit. "Prevention is not just better medicine; it's better economics."

Nutrition advocates called for expanded access to fresh food in underserved communities, often described as "food deserts," where residents may lack nearby grocery stores offering healthy options.

"You can't tell someone to eat more vegetables if the only store within miles is a gas station," one panelist noted.

Summit organizers outlined a multi-pronged strategy including improved nutrition education, revised food labeling, investment in community recreation infrastructure, and policy reforms targeting the marketing of unhealthy products to children.

While the challenges remain daunting, participants expressed cautious optimism that coordinated action across government, healthcare, and private sectors could begin to reverse decades of rising rates.

"This is solvable," Clinton said in closing. "But only if we commit to it together."

# CNN Fit Nation: Summit Tackles America's Growing Obesity Crisis

*Health experts, policymakers, and advocates gather to confront a national epidemic*

---

**By CNN Health Staff**

WASHINGTON — Health leaders, policy experts, and community advocates convened this week for a landmark summit addressing one of America's most pressing public health challenges: the obesity epidemic affecting millions of children and adults across the nation.

The gathering, part of the ongoing Fit Nation initiative, brought together diverse voices united by a common goal—reversing troubling trends that have seen obesity rates climb steadily over the past several decades.

## A Nation at a Crossroads

Recent data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention paints a sobering picture. More than 40% of American adults and roughly one in five children now meet the clinical definition of obesity, a condition linked to heart disease, type 2 diabetes, certain cancers, and other serious health complications.

"We're not just talking about numbers on a scale," said one summit participant during the opening session. "We're talking about the long-term health and economic future of an entire generation."

The economic stakes are significant. Obesity-related healthcare costs the United States an estimated $170 billion annually, a figure that continues to rise as the crisis deepens.

## Beyond Personal Responsibility

A central theme emerging from the summit was the shift away from framing obesity solely as a matter of individual willpower. Instead, speakers emphasized the complex web of factors contributing to the epidemic.

"Food deserts, aggressive marketing of ultra-processed foods, sedentary lifestyles, and socioeconomic barriers all play a role," explained a public health researcher addressing attendees. "Solutions must be as multifaceted as the problem itself."

Participants pointed to structural challenges, including limited access to fresh, affordable produce in low-income communities and the disappearance of physical education programs from many schools.

## Policy Solutions on the Table

The summit's working sessions generated a range of policy proposals aimed at both prevention and treatment:

**School-based interventions:** Advocates called for restoring robust physical education programs and improving the nutritional quality of school meals, which for many children represent their most reliable source of daily nutrition.

**Urban planning reforms:** Several experts highlighted the importance of "built environments" that encourage physical activity—safe sidewalks, accessible parks, and bike-friendly infrastructure.

**Food policy changes:** Discussions included proposals to regulate marketing of unhealthy foods to children, expand access to fresh food in underserved areas, and reconsider agricultural subsidies.

**Healthcare access:** Panelists debated expanding insurance coverage for obesity treatment, including nutritional counseling and, increasingly, new medications that have shown promise in weight management.

## The Role of New Treatments

The recent emergence of GLP-1 medications sparked considerable discussion among attendees. While acknowledging their effectiveness, experts cautioned against viewing pharmaceutical interventions as a standalone solution.

"These medications can be transformative for many patients," a physician noted, "but access, cost, and long-term sustainability remain significant concerns. We can't medicate our way out of a systemic problem."

## Community Voices

Perhaps most compelling were the personal stories shared throughout the summit. Community organizers described grassroots efforts that have shown measurable success—from urban gardening initiatives to after-school fitness programs.

One advocate described transforming a vacant lot into a thriving community garden that now provides fresh vegetables to hundreds of families while teaching children about nutrition.

"Change happens at the local level," she said. "When people feel ownership over their health and their community, that's when we see real results."

## Looking Ahead

As the summit concluded, organizers stressed that meaningful progress will require sustained commitment across sectors—government, healthcare, education, and private industry.

"There's no single silver bullet," one closing speaker acknowledged. "But if we align our policies, invest in our communities, and treat this as the public health emergency it truly is, we can bend the curve."

The Fit Nation initiative plans to continue its work through community programs, educational campaigns, and ongoing dialogue with policymakers.

For millions of American families, the outcome of these efforts could mean the difference between a healthier future and a continuing crisis.

---

*This story is part of CNN's Fit Nation series, dedicated to helping Americans lead healthier lives.*

# Health Leaders Gather at CNN Fit Nation Summit to Combat America's Obesity Crisis

## Experts, Officials, and Advocates Address Nation's Growing Weight Problem

Health experts, policymakers, and advocates convened at the CNN Fit Nation Summit to tackle one of America's most pressing public health challenges: the nation's escalating obesity epidemic. The summit brought together diverse voices to examine the scope of the problem and debate potential solutions, from dietary regulations to youth-focused initiatives.

## Sobering Statistics Frame the Crisis

Speakers presented data underscoring the severity of the obesity problem in the United States. According to figures cited at the summit, roughly two-thirds of American adults are overweight or obese, with obesity rates having more than doubled among adults since the 1970s.

Perhaps most alarming were statistics regarding childhood obesity. Experts noted that the percentage of overweight children and adolescents has climbed dramatically over recent decades, raising concerns about a generation potentially facing shorter lifespans than their parents—a reversal of historical trends.

Health officials emphasized the associated risks, including elevated rates of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, and certain cancers. The economic burden was also highlighted, with obesity-related healthcare costs running into the tens of billions of dollars annually.

## The Trans Fat Debate

A significant portion of the summit focused on the contentious issue of trans fats in the American diet. Nutrition experts argued that artificial trans fats, found in many processed and fried foods, contribute to raised levels of LDL ("bad") cholesterol while lowering HDL ("good") cholesterol.

Advocates for regulation pointed to municipal efforts, such as restrictions implemented in cities like New York, as models for reducing trans fat consumption. Supporters argued that removing artificial trans fats from restaurant food and processed products could prevent thousands of heart-related deaths.

However, the debate revealed tensions. Some industry representatives and free-market advocates cautioned against government overreach, arguing that consumer education and voluntary reformulation by food companies represented more appropriate approaches than mandates. Questions were raised about whether substitute ingredients would prove healthier and about the practical challenges facing small restaurants.

## Clinton's Alliance for a Healthier Generation

A centerpiece of the summit was discussion of the Alliance for a Healthier Generation, a partnership founded by the Clinton Foundation and the American Heart Association. The initiative, championed by former President Bill Clinton, focuses on combating childhood obesity through systemic changes.

The Alliance gained attention for negotiating agreements with major beverage companies to limit high-calorie sugary drinks in schools, replacing them with healthier options like water, low-fat milk, and smaller portions of juice. The program also worked with schools to improve nutritional standards and increase physical activity opportunities.

Clinton, who has spoken personally about his own health struggles, framed the effort as a matter of giving children the tools to live healthier lives. Supporters praised the public-private partnership model for achieving voluntary industry cooperation without relying solely on legislation.

## Looking Ahead

The summit concluded with calls for continued collaboration among government, industry, healthcare providers, schools, and families. While participants disagreed on the appropriate balance between regulation and personal responsibility, there was broad consensus that the obesity epidemic demands sustained, multifaceted attention.

As one speaker noted, reversing decades of troubling health trends will require not a single solution but a coordinated effort across all levels of society—a challenge that the Fit Nation Summit sought to illuminate and advance.
